basics.name: John Jamieson
basics.label: Data & BI Analyst — Financial Systems
basics.summary: Data and BI analyst who builds the reporting, dashboards, and automated data processes that businesses run on. Strong SQL foundation — currently writing SQL every day against MS SQL Server in financial services — with a decade of turning messy financial and operational data into reliable, decision-ready datasets. Pairs hands-on data work (SQL, BI/reporting, automation) with deep finance-domain knowledge that most data candidates don't have.

work.name: First National
highlights: Write SQL against MS SQL Server for ad-hoc reporting and data-extract requests: 30+ resolved in just over six months across 5+ business areas, including mortgage operations, broker relationships, residential taxes, and transformation projects.

Turn vague requests into testable report definitions (source, grain, date logic, status and duplicate rules); e.g., delivered a 459-event, 288-transaction document-activity report from undocumented application data as an auditable Excel extract.

Reconstructed historical identifier changes for 300+ records from field-level audit logs with read-only SQL; normalized inconsistent null and placeholder values, preserved multi-step histories, and resolved every populated record.

Built a 13+ field insured-mortgage audit report for a major bank client, refined through multiple stakeholder review rounds, matched to application screens, and saved as reusable SQL for repeat pulls.

Designed and prototyped an AI-assisted semantic search over historical ticket data (vector embeddings / retrieval-augmented generation) to turn operational history into a reusable knowledge base; evaluated local vs. API embedding options against security and tooling constraints and documented the architecture and blockers.

Build and maintain documentation, queries, and data/knowledge assets used across a cross-functional team; proposed a business-function-based model for application health monitoring of a complex, undocumented environment.

websiteHighlights.long: One request gave me only a few document identifiers and a start date, for an application whose data wasn't documented. I worked out how deal requests, document details and document definitions link from SQL Server's metadata and the application's configuration, then wrote the report's definition down before the query: its source, one row per generation event, how each status counts, and how duplicates are handled. Along the way I caught an identifier mapping that would have dropped one form, and kept subordinate reports from being counted twice. The result was an auditable Excel extract of 459 events across 288 transactions, with the SQL kept so it can be reproduced.
